accounts.prose: Provides the shared single-attempt execution boundary used by policies: it awaits a callback, classifies returned values and thrown errors with injected filters, reports timed success/failure events, and returns a tagged outcome for policy-specific control flow. It does not itself retry, delay, fall back, time out, or limit concurrency; those decisions remain with callers.

qualifications: Interpretation of first-observed TypeScript source; runtime, loader, and deployment behavior were not executed.

Incoming dependency analysis establishes static imports, not every caller's runtime use. Retry and no-op integration were inspected directly; bulkhead, fallback, timeout, and circuit-breaker internals were not.

accounts.prose: FailureOrSuccess is the policy FailureReason union plus `{success}`. returnOrThrow collapses it for simple callers: throw `{error}`, return `{success}`, otherwise return the filtered failure value. This lets richer policies inspect failures while no-op-style callers recover ordinary return/throw semantics.

accounts.prose: ExecuteWrapper owns fresh success/failure emitters and exposes their subscription functions. invoke awaits the callback. A value rejected by resultFilter becomes a handled failure `{value}`; any other value becomes `{success}`. A thrown error matching errorFilter becomes `{error}`; a nonmatching error is reported as unhandled and rethrown. clone preserves the two predicates but creates new emitters.

qualifications: “Fresh emitters” follows construction of a new ExecuteWrapper in clone; filter functions themselves are reused.
The callback may be synchronous or promise-like because its result is awaited.

accounts.prose: ExecuteWrapper is a boundary around one attempted call: it normalizes outcomes that a policy is meant to handle into a discriminated object, while allowing an unhandled thrown error to remain an actual rejection. `invoke(fn, ...args)` awaits `fn(...args)`, so the same classification applies to direct return values and fulfilled promises. After fulfillment, `resultFilter(value) === false` produces `{ success: value }`; `true` treats the otherwise successful value as a handled failure and produces `{ value }`. If the attempted work throws or its promise rejects, `errorFilter(error) === true` converts that exception to `{ error }`; `false` emits an unhandled-failure notification when observed and then rethrows the original error. Thus “handled” means represented for policy-level processing, not necessarily that the overall operation ultimately succeeds. With the constructor defaults, no returned value is rejected by result filtering and no thrown error is handled.

accounts.prose: The wrapper does not itself retry, delay, or turn a handled failure into the caller's final return value. RetryPolicy supplies that higher-level meaning: `{success}` ends its loop; `{error}` or `{value}` is passed to backoff as the last failure and may trigger another attempt. Once retries are unavailable, RetryPolicy rethrows the stored error for `{error}`, but returns the stored value for `{value}`. @investigram-90eca545 · interpretation
ExecuteWrapper is a boundary around one attempted call: it normalizes outcomes that a policy is meant to handle into a discriminated object, while allowing an unhandled thrown error to remain an actual rejection. `invoke(fn, ...args)` awaits `fn(...args)`, so the same classification applies to direct return values and fulfilled promises. After fulfillment, `resultFilter(value) === false` produces `{ success: value }`; `true` treats the otherwise successful value as a handled failure and produces `{ value }`. Thus “handled” means represented for policy-level processing, not necessarily that the overall operation ultimately succeeds. With the constructor defaults, no returned value is rejected by result filtering and no thrown error is handled.

accounts.prose: ExecuteWrapper is a boundary around one attempted call: it normalizes outcomes that a policy is meant to handle into a discriminated object, while allowing an unhandled thrown error to remain an actual rejection. `invoke(fn, ...args)` awaits `fn(...args)`, so the same classification applies to direct return values and fulfilled promises. After fulfillment, `resultFilter(value) === false` produces `{ success: value }`; `true` treats the otherwise successful value as a handled failure and produces `{ value }`. If the attempted work throws or its promise rejects, `errorFilter(error) === true` converts that exception to `{ error }`; `false` emits an unhandled-failure notification when observed and then rethrows the original error. Thus “handled” means represented for policy-level processing, not necessarily that the overall operation ultimately succeeds. With the constructor defaults, no returned value is rejected by result filtering and no thrown error is handled.

accounts.prose: The two public event properties are subscription functions, not the outcome itself. A success notification contains only elapsed `duration`. A failure notification contains `duration`, `handled`, and `reason`, where `reason` is `{ value }` for a filtered result or `{ error }` for an exception. For a filtered result, `handled` is always true. For an exception, it is the boolean returned by `errorFilter`, so an event can report `handled: false` immediately before `invoke` rethrows. Timing work is skipped entirely when both emitters have zero listeners at the start of the invocation; consequently, these events are observational and listener presence controls whether duration is measured. Subscriptions return disposables, and EventEmitter invokes current listeners synchronously.

referent.description: ExecuteWrapper success/failure event payloads and conditional duration measurement

qualifications: Listener count is sampled once, before the callback is invoked; adding a first listener during that callback does not retroactively enable timing for that invocation.

The duration covers the awaited callback plus subsequent result filtering up to the emission point, and is expressed in milliseconds by either `performance.now()` or a converted high-resolution process clock.

EventEmitter does not catch listener exceptions. In ExecuteWrapper, filtering and emission occur inside its `try`, so a throwing filter or listener can alter the apparent failure path; in particular, this code does not provide observer-exception isolation.

Because each instance initializes its own success and failure emitters, listeners attached to the original are not attached to the clone. This lets a policy variant retain the same classification rules without sharing event subscriptions.

accounts.prose: The wrapper does not itself retry, delay, or turn a handled failure into the caller's final return value. RetryPolicy supplies that higher-level meaning: `{success}` ends its loop; `{error}` or `{value}` is passed to backoff as the last failure and may trigger another attempt. Once retries are unavailable, RetryPolicy rethrows the stored error for `{error}`, but returns the stored value for `{value}`. This explains why a result-filtered value is called a failure for policy decisions even though it can eventually be returned to the caller after give-up.

accounts.prose: ExecuteWrapper owns fresh success/failure emitters and exposes their subscription functions. invoke awaits the callback. A value rejected by resultFilter becomes a handled failure `{value}`; any other value becomes `{success}`. A thrown error matching errorFilter becomes `{error}`; a nonmatching error is reported as unhandled and rethrown. clone preserves the two predicates but creates new emitters.

referent.description: ExecuteWrapper classification and invocation mechanism

qualifications: “Fresh emitters” follows construction of a new ExecuteWrapper in clone; filter functions themselves are reused.
The callback may be synchronous or promise-like because its result is awaited.

accounts.prose: ExecuteWrapper is a boundary around one attempted call: it normalizes outcomes that a policy is meant to handle into a discriminated object, while allowing an unhandled thrown error to remain an actual rejection. `invoke(fn, ...args)` awaits `fn(...args)`, so the same classification applies to direct return values and fulfilled promises. After fulfillment, `resultFilter(value) === false` produces `{ success: value }`; `true` treats the otherwise successful value as a handled failure and produces `{ value }`. If the attempted work throws or its promise rejects, `errorFilter(error) === true` converts that exception to `{ error }`; `false` emits an unhandled-failure notification when observed and then rethrows the original error. Thus “handled” means represented for policy-level processing, not necessarily that the overall operation ultimately succeeds. With the constructor defaults, no returned value is rejected by result filtering and no thrown error is handled.

referent.description: Clarified ExecuteWrapper invocation, outcome classification, observability, and cloning behavior

qualifications: This describes the captured TypeScript implementation; source text alone does not establish behavior in every built or deployed version.
The ordinary outcome flow assumes the supplied filters and event listeners do not themselves throw; those callbacks are not isolated from `invoke`'s control flow.
`await` assimilates native promises and other PromiseLike results before result filtering.

accounts.prose: The two public event properties are subscription functions, not the outcome itself. A success notification contains only elapsed `duration`. A failure notification contains `duration`, `handled`, and `reason`, where `reason` is `{ value }` for a filtered result or `{ error }` for an exception. For a filtered result, `handled` is always true. For an exception, it is the boolean returned by `errorFilter`, so an event can report `handled: false` immediately before `invoke` rethrows. Timing work is skipped entirely when both emitters have zero listeners at the start of the invocation; consequently, these events are observational and listener presence controls whether duration is measured. Subscriptions return disposables, and EventEmitter invokes current listeners synchronously.

referent.description: ExecuteWrapper success/failure event payloads and conditional duration measurement

qualifications: Listener count is sampled once, before the callback is invoked; adding a first listener during that callback does not retroactively enable timing for that invocation.

The duration covers the awaited callback plus subsequent result filtering up to the emission point, and is expressed in milliseconds by either `performance.now()` or a converted high-resolution process clock.

EventEmitter does not catch listener exceptions. In ExecuteWrapper, filtering and emission occur inside its `try`, so a throwing filter or listener can alter the apparent failure path; in particular, this code does not provide observer-exception isolation.

accounts.prose: The wrapper does not itself retry, delay, or turn a handled failure into the caller's final return value. RetryPolicy supplies that higher-level meaning: `{success}` ends its loop; `{error}` or `{value}` is passed to backoff as the last failure and may trigger another attempt. Once retries are unavailable, RetryPolicy rethrows the stored error for `{error}`, but returns the stored value for `{value}`. This explains why a result-filtered value is called a failure for policy decisions even though it can eventually be returned to the caller after give-up.

referent.description: How RetryPolicy consumes ExecuteWrapper's classified outcomes

qualifications: This consumer behavior is specific to the captured RetryPolicy implementation and is not intrinsic to ExecuteWrapper's union type.
RetryPolicy also stops retrying when its abort signal is set or its configured retry bound is reached.

accounts.prose: ExecuteWrapper is a boundary around one attempted call: it normalizes outcomes that a policy is meant to handle into a discriminated object, while allowing an unhandled thrown error to remain an actual rejection. `invoke(fn, ...args)` awaits `fn(...args)`, so the same classification applies to direct return values and fulfilled promises. After fulfillment, `resultFilter(value) === false` produces `{ success: value }`; `true` treats the otherwise successful value as a handled failure and produces `{ value }`. If the attempted work throws or its promise rejects, `errorFilter(error) === true` converts that exception to `{ error }`; `false` emits an unhandled-failure notification when observed and then rethrows the original error. Thus “handled” means represented for policy-level processing, not necessarily that the overall operation ultimately succeeds. With the constructor defaults, no returned value is rejected by result filtering and no thrown error is handled.

accounts.prose: The two public event properties are subscription functions, not the outcome itself. A success notification contains only elapsed `duration`. A failure notification contains `duration`, `handled`, and `reason`, where `reason` is `{ value }` for a filtered result or `{ error }` for an exception. For a filtered result, `handled` is always true. For an exception, it is the boolean returned by `errorFilter`, so an event can report `handled: false` immediately before `invoke` rethrows. Timing work is skipped entirely when both emitters have zero listeners at the start of the invocation; consequently, these events are observational and listener presence controls whether duration is measured. Subscriptions return disposables, and EventEmitter invokes current listeners synchronously.

referent.description: ExecuteWrapper success/failure event payloads and conditional duration measurement

qualifications: Listener count is sampled once, before the callback is invoked; adding a first listener during that callback does not retroactively enable timing for that invocation.

The duration covers the awaited callback plus subsequent result filtering up to the emission point, and is expressed in milliseconds by either `performance.now()` or a converted high-resolution process clock.

EventEmitter does not catch listener exceptions. In ExecuteWrapper, filtering and emission occur inside its `try`, so a throwing filter or listener can alter the apparent failure path; in particular, this code does not provide observer-exception isolation.

accounts.prose: The wrapper does not itself retry, delay, or turn a handled failure into the caller's final return value. RetryPolicy supplies that higher-level meaning: `{success}` ends its loop; `{error}` or `{value}` is passed to backoff as the last failure and may trigger another attempt. Once retries are unavailable, RetryPolicy rethrows the stored error for `{error}`, but returns the stored value for `{value}`. This explains why a result-filtered value is called a failure for policy decisions even though it can eventually be returned to the caller after give-up.

accounts.prose: ExecuteWrapper.invoke classifies the value caught by its single try/catch, not merely exceptions originating in the supplied callback. After awaiting the callback, failures from resultFilter, duration measurement on the success path, or synchronous success listeners enter the same catch and are passed to errorFilter. If that predicate returns true, invoke emits a handled failure event and resolves to an object containing the exact caught value as `error`; if it returns false, invoke emits an unhandled failure event and rethrows that same value. This sharpens, rather than overturns, the earlier account: classification has important boundaries and can itself be disrupted by predicates, timing, and listeners.

The exact caught value is preserved only while errorFilter, failure-duration evaluation, and failure emission complete normally.

accounts.prose: Event notification is synchronous and has no listener-level exception isolation. A throwing success listener is caught by invoke and can cause a completed callback result to be discarded, passed to errorFilter as the listener's exception, and followed by a failure notification. By contrast, errorFilter and failure emission run inside the catch clause rather than inside another protective try: if errorFilter throws, its exception replaces the original caught value; if failure-duration evaluation or a failure listener throws, that later exception escapes and can prevent the selected `{ error }` result or original-value rethrow. With multiple listeners, EventEmitter stops iterating when one throws.

accounts.prose: ExecuteWrapper is a boundary around one attempted call: it normalizes outcomes that a policy is meant to handle into a discriminated object, while allowing an unhandled thrown error to remain an actual rejection. `invoke(fn, ...args)` awaits `fn(...args)`, so the same classification applies to direct return values and fulfilled promises. After fulfillment, `resultFilter(value) === false` produces `{ success: value }`; `true` treats the otherwise successful value as a handled failure and produces `{ value }`. If the attempted work throws or its promise rejects, `errorFilter(error) === true` converts that exception to `{ error }`; `false` emits an unhandled-failure notification when observed and then rethrows the original error. Thus “handled” means represented for policy-level processing, not necessarily that the overall operation ultimately succeeds. With the constructor defaults, no returned value is rejected by result filtering and no thrown error is handled.

accounts.prose: The two public event properties are subscription functions, not the outcome itself. A success notification contains only elapsed `duration`. A failure notification contains `duration`, `handled`, and `reason`, where `reason` is `{ value }` for a filtered result or `{ error }` for an exception. For a filtered result, `handled` is always true. For an exception, it is the boolean returned by `errorFilter`, so an event can report `handled: false` immediately before `invoke` rethrows. Timing work is skipped entirely when both emitters have zero listeners at the start of the invocation; consequently, these events are observational and listener presence controls whether duration is measured. Subscriptions return disposables, and EventEmitter invokes current listeners synchronously.

referent.description: ExecuteWrapper success/failure event payloads and conditional duration measurement

qualifications: Listener count is sampled once, before the callback is invoked; adding a first listener during that callback does not retroactively enable timing for that invocation.

The duration covers the awaited callback plus subsequent result filtering up to the emission point, and is expressed in milliseconds by either `performance.now()` or a converted high-resolution process clock.

EventEmitter does not catch listener exceptions. In ExecuteWrapper, filtering and emission occur inside its `try`, so a throwing filter or listener can alter the apparent failure path; in particular, this code does not provide observer-exception isolation.

accounts.prose: The wrapper does not itself retry, delay, or turn a handled failure into the caller's final return value. RetryPolicy supplies that higher-level meaning: `{success}` ends its loop; `{error}` or `{value}` is passed to backoff as the last failure and may trigger another attempt. Once retries are unavailable, RetryPolicy rethrows the stored error for `{error}`, but returns the stored value for `{value}`. This explains why a result-filtered value is called a failure for policy decisions even though it can eventually be returned to the caller after give-up.

@investigram-da67d827 · interpretation
ExecuteWrapper.invoke classifies the value caught by its single try/catch, not merely exceptions originating in the supplied callback. After awaiting the callback, failures from resultFilter, duration measurement on the success path, or synchronous success listeners enter the same catch and are passed to errorFilter. If that predicate returns true, invoke emits a handled failure event and resolves to an object containing the exact caught value as `error`; if it returns false, invoke emits an unhandled failure event and rethrows that same value. This sharpens, rather than overturns, the earlier account: classification has important boundaries and can itself be disrupted by predicates, timing, and listeners.

  Qualification: The true/false wording follows the declared boolean predicate contract; ordinary JavaScript branching would in practice use the returned value's truthiness if the contract were violated.

@investigram-92cfd159 · interpretation
Event notification is synchronous and has no listener-level exception isolation. A throwing success listener is caught by invoke and can cause a completed callback result to be discarded, passed to errorFilter as the listener's exception, and followed by a failure notification. By contrast, errorFilter and failure emission run inside the catch clause rather than inside another protective try: if errorFilter throws, its exception replaces the original caught value; if failure-duration evaluation or a failure listener throws, that later exception escapes and can prevent the selected `{ error }` result or original-value rethrow. With multiple listeners, EventEmitter stops iterating when one throws.
Referent: Observer and classifier failures that alter ExecuteWrapper exception outcomes

A thrown error matching errorFilter becomes `{error}`; a nonmatching error is reported as unhandled and rethrown. clone preserves the two predicates but creates new emitters.

accounts.prose: ExecuteWrapper is a boundary around one attempted call: it normalizes outcomes that a policy is meant to handle into a discriminated object, while allowing an unhandled thrown error to remain an actual rejection. `invoke(fn, ...args)` awaits `fn(...args)`, so the same classification applies to direct return values and fulfilled promises. After fulfillment, `resultFilter(value) === false` produces `{ success: value }`; `true` treats the otherwise successful value as a handled failure and produces `{ value }`. If the attempted work throws or its promise rejects, `errorFilter(error) === true` converts that exception to `{ error }`; `false` emits an unhandled-failure notification when observed and then rethrows the original error. Thus “handled” means represented for policy-level processing, not necessarily that the overall operation ultimately succeeds. With the constructor defaults, no returned value is rejected by result filtering and no thrown error is handled.

accounts.prose: The two public event properties are subscription functions, not the outcome itself. A success notification contains only elapsed `duration`. A failure notification contains `duration`, `handled`, and `reason`, where `reason` is `{ value }` for a filtered result or `{ error }` for an exception. For a filtered result, `handled` is always true. For an exception, it is the boolean returned by `errorFilter`, so an event can report `handled: false` immediately before `invoke` rethrows. Timing work is skipped entirely when both emitters have zero listeners at the start of the invocation; consequently, these events are observational and listener presence controls whether duration is measured. Subscriptions return disposables, and EventEmitter invokes current listeners synchronously.

referent.description: ExecuteWrapper success/failure event payloads and conditional duration measurement

qualifications: Listener count is sampled once, before the callback is invoked; adding a first listener during that callback does not retroactively enable timing for that invocation.

The duration covers the awaited callback plus subsequent result filtering up to the emission point, and is expressed in milliseconds by either `performance.now()` or a converted high-resolution process clock.

EventEmitter does not catch listener exceptions. In ExecuteWrapper, filtering and emission occur inside its `try`, so a throwing filter or listener can alter the apparent failure path; in particular, this code does not provide observer-exception isolation.

accounts.prose: The wrapper does not itself retry, delay, or turn a handled failure into the caller's final return value. RetryPolicy supplies that higher-level meaning: `{success}` ends its loop; `{error}` or `{value}` is passed to backoff as the last failure and may trigger another attempt. Once retries are unavailable, RetryPolicy rethrows the stored error for `{error}`, but returns the stored value for `{value}`. This explains why a result-filtered value is called a failure for policy decisions even though it can eventually be returned to the caller after give-up.

qualifications: This consumer behavior is specific to the captured RetryPolicy implementation and is not intrinsic to ExecuteWrapper's union type.
RetryPolicy also stops retrying when its abort signal is set or its configured retry bound is reached.

accounts.prose: ExecuteWrapper.invoke classifies the value caught by its single try/catch, not merely exceptions originating in the supplied callback. After awaiting the callback, failures from resultFilter, duration measurement on the success path, or synchronous success listeners enter the same catch and are passed to errorFilter. If that predicate returns true, invoke emits a handled failure event and resolves to an object containing the exact caught value as `error`; if it returns false, invoke emits an unhandled failure event and rethrows that same value. This sharpens, rather than overturns, the earlier account: classification has important boundaries and can itself be disrupted by predicates, timing, and listeners.

referent.description: Deep examination of ExecuteWrapper exception classification and its boundaries

qualifications: These are static-source findings; no execution was performed, and source alone does not establish observed runtime behavior in every deployment.
The true/false wording follows the declared boolean predicate contract; ordinary JavaScript branching would in practice use the returned value's truthiness if the contract were violated.
The exact caught value is preserved only while errorFilter, failure-duration evaluation, and failure emission complete normally.

accounts.prose: Event notification is synchronous and has no listener-level exception isolation. A throwing success listener is caught by invoke and can cause a completed callback result to be discarded, passed to errorFilter as the listener's exception, and followed by a failure notification. By contrast, errorFilter and failure emission run inside the catch clause rather than inside another protective try: if errorFilter throws, its exception replaces the original caught value; if failure-duration evaluation or a failure listener throws, that later exception escapes and can prevent the selected `{ error }` result or original-value rethrow. With multiple listeners, EventEmitter stops iterating when one throws.

referent.description: Observer and classifier failures that alter ExecuteWrapper exception outcomes

qualifications: A failure event is attempted before either returning `{ error }` or rethrowing the unhandled value, provided timing evaluation and emission complete normally.
Listener registration changes during an awaited call can affect who receives an event, while the decision to collect timing and emit at all is fixed by listener counts at invocation start.
These edge cases follow control flow in the captured sources and are not covered by the supplied ExecuteWrapper test file.

qualifications: Its emit method directly invokes listeners in registration order and does not catch their exceptions.

accounts.prose: The catch domain starts at `await fn(...args)` and extends through result filtering, success-duration calculation, and success-event emission. It therefore handles both synchronous throws and awaited rejections from the callback, but it also reclassifies infrastructure failures from resultFilter or the success path as though they were operation errors. Stopwatch creation occurs before the try, so an exception while initially reading the clock bypasses errorFilter entirely.

referent.description: Operations included in and excluded from ExecuteWrapper's catch domain

qualifications: The implementation awaits a PromiseLike or immediate result, so the caught rejection reason need not be an Error object.
The stopwatch is created only when at least one success or failure listener exists at invocation start; without such a listener, timing and event emission are skipped.
No supplied test in the directly dependent Executor test module exercises rejected promises, throwing filters, timing failures, or throwing listeners.

accounts.prose: ExecuteWrapper is a boundary around one attempted call: it normalizes outcomes that a policy is meant to handle into a discriminated object, while allowing an unhandled thrown error to remain an actual rejection. `invoke(fn, ...args)` awaits `fn(...args)`, so the same classification applies to direct return values and fulfilled promises. After fulfillment, `resultFilter(value) === false` produces `{ success: value }`; `true` treats the otherwise successful value as a handled failure and produces `{ value }`. If the attempted work throws or its promise rejects, `errorFilter(error) === true` converts that exception to `{ error }`; `false` emits an unhandled-failure notification when observed and then rethrows the original error. Thus “handled” means represented for policy-level processing, not necessarily that the overall operation ultimately succeeds. With the constructor defaults, no returned value is rejected by result filtering and no thrown error is handled.

The ordinary outcome flow assumes the supplied filters and event listeners do not themselves throw; those callbacks are not isolated from `invoke`'s control flow.
`await` assimilates native promises and other PromiseLike results before result filtering.

accounts.prose: The two public event properties are subscription functions, not the outcome itself. A success notification contains only elapsed `duration`. A failure notification contains `duration`, `handled`, and `reason`, where `reason` is `{ value }` for a filtered result or `{ error }` for an exception. For a filtered result, `handled` is always true. For an exception, it is the boolean returned by `errorFilter`, so an event can report `handled: false` immediately before `invoke` rethrows. Timing work is skipped entirely when both emitters have zero listeners at the start of the invocation; consequently, these events are observational and listener presence controls whether duration is measured. Subscriptions return disposables, and EventEmitter invokes current listeners synchronously.

referent.description: ExecuteWrapper success/failure event payloads and conditional duration measurement

qualifications: Listener count is sampled once, before the callback is invoked; adding a first listener during that callback does not retroactively enable timing for that invocation.

The duration covers the awaited callback plus subsequent result filtering up to the emission point, and is expressed in milliseconds by either `performance.now()` or a converted high-resolution process clock.

EventEmitter does not catch listener exceptions. In ExecuteWrapper, filtering and emission occur inside its `try`, so a throwing filter or listener can alter the apparent failure path; in particular, this code does not provide observer-exception isolation.

accounts.prose: The wrapper does not itself retry, delay, or turn a handled failure into the caller's final return value. RetryPolicy supplies that higher-level meaning: `{success}` ends its loop; `{error}` or `{value}` is passed to backoff as the last failure and may trigger another attempt. Once retries are unavailable, RetryPolicy rethrows the stored error for `{error}`, but returns the stored value for `{value}`. This explains why a result-filtered value is called a failure for policy decisions even though it can eventually be returned to the caller after give-up.

qualifications: This consumer behavior is specific to the captured RetryPolicy implementation and is not intrinsic to ExecuteWrapper's union type.

@investigram-da67d827 · interpretation
ExecuteWrapper.invoke classifies the value caught by its single try/catch, not merely exceptions originating in the supplied callback. After awaiting the callback, failures from resultFilter, duration measurement on the success path, or synchronous success listeners enter the same catch and are passed to errorFilter. If that predicate returns true, invoke emits a handled failure event and resolves to an object containing the exact caught value as `error`; if it returns false, invoke emits an unhandled failure event and rethrows that same value. This sharpens, rather than overturns, the earlier account: classification has important boundaries and can itself be disrupted by predicates, timing, and listeners.

  Qualification: The true/false wording follows the declared boolean predicate contract; ordinary JavaScript branching would in practice use the returned value's truthiness if the contract were violated.
  Qualification: The exact caught value is preserved only while errorFilter, failure-duration evaluation, and failure emission complete normally.

@investigram-92cfd159 · interpretation
Event notification is synchronous and has no listener-level exception isolation. A throwing success listener is caught by invoke and can cause a completed callback result to be discarded, passed to errorFilter as the listener's exception, and followed by a failure notification. By contrast, errorFilter and failure emission run inside the catch clause rather than inside another protective try: if errorFilter throws, its exception replaces the original caught value; if failure-duration evaluation or a failure listener throws, that later exception escapes and can prevent the selected `{ error }` result or original-value rethrow. With multiple listeners, EventEmitter stops iterating when one throws.
Referent: Observer and classifier failures that alter ExecuteWrapper exception outcomes
  Qualification: A failure event is attempted before either returning `{ error }` or rethrowing the unhandled value, provided timing evaluation and emission complete normally.
  Qualification: Listener registration changes during an awaited call can affect who receives an event, while the decision to collect timing and emit at all is fixed by listener counts at invocation start.
  Qualification: These edge cases follow control flow in the captured sources and are not covered by the supplied ExecuteWrapper test file.

The catch domain starts at `await fn(...args)` and extends through result filtering, success-duration calculation, and success-event emission. It therefore handles both synchronous throws and awaited rejections from the callback, but it also reclassifies infrastructure failures from resultFilter or the success path as though they were operation errors. Stopwatch creation occurs before the try, so an exception while initially reading the clock bypasses errorFilter entirely.

accounts.prose: ExecuteWrapper is a boundary around one attempted call: it normalizes outcomes that a policy is meant to handle into a discriminated object, while allowing an unhandled thrown error to remain an actual rejection. `invoke(fn, ...args)` awaits `fn(...args)`, so the same classification applies to direct return values and fulfilled promises. After fulfillment, `resultFilter(value) === false` produces `{ success: value }`; `true` treats the otherwise successful value as a handled failure and produces `{ value }`. If the attempted work throws or its promise rejects, `errorFilter(error) === true` converts that exception to `{ error }`; `false` emits an unhandled-failure notification when observed and then rethrows the original error. Thus “handled” means represented for policy-level processing, not necessarily that the overall operation ultimately succeeds. With the constructor defaults, no returned value is rejected by result filtering and no thrown error is handled.

referent.description: Clarified ExecuteWrapper invocation, outcome classification, observability, and cloning behavior

qualifications: This describes the captured TypeScript implementation; source text alone does not establish behavior in every built or deployed version.
The ordinary outcome flow assumes the supplied filters and event listeners do not themselves throw; those callbacks are not isolated from `invoke`'s control flow.
`await` assimilates native promises and other PromiseLike results before result filtering.

accounts.prose: The two public event properties are subscription functions, not the outcome itself. A success notification contains only elapsed `duration`. A failure notification contains `duration`, `handled`, and `reason`, where `reason` is `{ value }` for a filtered result or `{ error }` for an exception. For a filtered result, `handled` is always true. For an exception, it is the boolean returned by `errorFilter`, so an event can report `handled: false` immediately before `invoke` rethrows. Timing work is skipped entirely when both emitters have zero listeners at the start of the invocation; consequently, these events are observational and listener presence controls whether duration is measured. Subscriptions return disposables, and EventEmitter invokes current listeners synchronously.

referent.description: ExecuteWrapper success/failure event payloads and conditional duration measurement

qualifications: Listener count is sampled once, before the callback is invoked; adding a first listener during that callback does not retroactively enable timing for that invocation.

The duration covers the awaited callback plus subsequent result filtering up to the emission point, and is expressed in milliseconds by either `performance.now()` or a converted high-resolution process clock.

EventEmitter does not catch listener exceptions. In ExecuteWrapper, filtering and emission occur inside its `try`, so a throwing filter or listener can alter the apparent failure path; in particular, this code does not provide observer-exception isolation.

accounts.prose: `clone()` copies configuration but not observation state. It constructs a new ExecuteWrapper with the same `errorFilter` and `resultFilter` function objects. Because each instance initializes its own success and failure emitters, listeners attached to the original are not attached to the clone. This lets a policy variant retain the same classification rules without sharing event subscriptions.

qualifications: The predicates are reused by reference rather than duplicated; any behavior arising from mutable state captured by those functions is therefore still shared.

accounts.prose: The wrapper does not itself retry, delay, or turn a handled failure into the caller's final return value. RetryPolicy supplies that higher-level meaning: `{success}` ends its loop; `{error}` or `{value}` is passed to backoff as the last failure and may trigger another attempt. Once retries are unavailable, RetryPolicy rethrows the stored error for `{error}`, but returns the stored value for `{value}`. This explains why a result-filtered value is called a failure for policy decisions even though it can eventually be returned to the caller after give-up.

qualifications: This consumer behavior is specific to the captured RetryPolicy implementation and is not intrinsic to ExecuteWrapper's union type.
RetryPolicy also stops retrying when its abort signal is set or its configured retry bound is reached.

accounts.prose: ExecuteWrapper is a boundary around one attempted call: it normalizes outcomes that a policy is meant to handle into a discriminated object, while allowing an unhandled thrown error to remain an actual rejection. `invoke(fn, ...args)` awaits `fn(...args)`, so the same classification applies to direct return values and fulfilled promises. After fulfillment, `resultFilter(value) === false` produces `{ success: value }`; `true` treats the otherwise successful value as a handled failure and produces `{ value }`. If the attempted work throws or its promise rejects, `errorFilter(error) === true` converts that exception to `{ error }`; `false` emits an unhandled-failure notification when observed and then rethrows the original error. Thus “handled” means represented for policy-level processing, not necessarily that the overall operation ultimately succeeds. With the constructor defaults, no returned value is rejected by result filtering and no thrown error is handled.

accounts.prose: The two public event properties are subscription functions, not the outcome itself. A success notification contains only elapsed `duration`. A failure notification contains `duration`, `handled`, and `reason`, where `reason` is `{ value }` for a filtered result or `{ error }` for an exception. For a filtered result, `handled` is always true. For an exception, it is the boolean returned by `errorFilter`, so an event can report `handled: false` immediately before `invoke` rethrows. Timing work is skipped entirely when both emitters have zero listeners at the start of the invocation; consequently, these events are observational and listener presence controls whether duration is measured. Subscriptions return disposables, and EventEmitter invokes current listeners synchronously.

referent.description: ExecuteWrapper success/failure event payloads and conditional duration measurement

qualifications: Listener count is sampled once, before the callback is invoked; adding a first listener during that callback does not retroactively enable timing for that invocation.

The duration covers the awaited callback plus subsequent result filtering up to the emission point, and is expressed in milliseconds by either `performance.now()` or a converted high-resolution process clock.

EventEmitter does not catch listener exceptions. In ExecuteWrapper, filtering and emission occur inside its `try`, so a throwing filter or listener can alter the apparent failure path; in particular, this code does not provide observer-exception isolation.

accounts.prose: `clone()` copies configuration but not observation state. It constructs a new ExecuteWrapper with the same `errorFilter` and `resultFilter` function objects. Because each instance initializes its own success and failure emitters, listeners attached to the original are not attached to the clone. This lets a policy variant retain the same classification rules without sharing event subscriptions.

referent.description: ExecuteWrapper clone configuration and listener isolation

qualifications: The predicates are reused by reference rather than duplicated; any behavior arising from mutable state captured by those functions is therefore still shared.
Fresh emitter state follows from constructing a new instance whose emitter fields are initialized per instance.

accounts.prose: The wrapper does not itself retry, delay, or turn a handled failure into the caller's final return value. RetryPolicy supplies that higher-level meaning: `{success}` ends its loop; `{error}` or `{value}` is passed to backoff as the last failure and may trigger another attempt. Once retries are unavailable, RetryPolicy rethrows the stored error for `{error}`, but returns the stored value for `{value}`. This explains why a result-filtered value is called a failure for policy decisions even though it can eventually be returned to the caller after give-up.

referent.description: How RetryPolicy consumes ExecuteWrapper's classified outcomes

qualifications: This consumer behavior is specific to the captured RetryPolicy implementation and is not intrinsic to ExecuteWrapper's union type.
RetryPolicy also stops retrying when its abort signal is set or its configured retry bound is reached.

accounts.prose: ExecuteWrapper owns fresh success/failure emitters and exposes their subscription functions. invoke awaits the callback. A value rejected by resultFilter becomes a handled failure `{value}`; any other value becomes `{success}`. A thrown error matching errorFilter becomes `{error}`; a nonmatching error is reported as unhandled and rethrown. clone preserves the two predicates but creates new emitters.

referent.description: ExecuteWrapper classification and invocation mechanism

qualifications: “Fresh emitters” follows construction of a new ExecuteWrapper in clone; filter functions themselves are reused.
The callback may be synchronous or promise-like because its result is awaited.

accounts.prose: ExecuteWrapper is a boundary around one attempted call: it normalizes outcomes that a policy is meant to handle into a discriminated object, while allowing an unhandled thrown error to remain an actual rejection. `invoke(fn, ...args)` awaits `fn(...args)`, so the same classification applies to direct return values and fulfilled promises. After fulfillment, `resultFilter(value) === false` produces `{ success: value }`; `true` treats the otherwise successful value as a handled failure and produces `{ value }`. If the attempted work throws or its promise rejects, `errorFilter(error) === true` converts that exception to `{ error }`; `false` emits an unhandled-failure notification when observed and then rethrows the original error. Thus “handled” means represented for policy-level processing, not necessarily that the overall operation ultimately succeeds. With the constructor defaults, no returned value is rejected by result filtering and no thrown error is handled.

referent.description: Clarified ExecuteWrapper invocation, outcome classification, observability, and cloning behavior

qualifications: This describes the captured TypeScript implementation; source text alone does not establish behavior in every built or deployed version.
The ordinary outcome flow assumes the supplied filters and event listeners do not themselves throw; those callbacks are not isolated from `invoke`'s control flow.
`await` assimilates native promises and other PromiseLike results before result filtering.

accounts.prose: The two public event properties are subscription functions, not the outcome itself. A success notification contains only elapsed `duration`. A failure notification contains `duration`, `handled`, and `reason`, where `reason` is `{ value }` for a filtered result or `{ error }` for an exception. For a filtered result, `handled` is always true. For an exception, it is the boolean returned by `errorFilter`, so an event can report `handled: false` immediately before `invoke` rethrows. Timing work is skipped entirely when both emitters have zero listeners at the start of the invocation; consequently, these events are observational and listener presence controls whether duration is measured. Subscriptions return disposables, and EventEmitter invokes current listeners synchronously.

referent.description: ExecuteWrapper success/failure event payloads and conditional duration measurement

qualifications: Listener count is sampled once, before the callback is invoked; adding a first listener during that callback does not retroactively enable timing for that invocation.

The duration covers the awaited callback plus subsequent result filtering up to the emission point, and is expressed in milliseconds by either `performance.now()` or a converted high-resolution process clock.

EventEmitter does not catch listener exceptions. In ExecuteWrapper, filtering and emission occur inside its `try`, so a throwing filter or listener can alter the apparent failure path; in particular, this code does not provide observer-exception isolation.

accounts.prose: `clone()` copies configuration but not observation state. It constructs a new ExecuteWrapper with the same `errorFilter` and `resultFilter` function objects. Because each instance initializes its own success and failure emitters, listeners attached to the original are not attached to the clone. This lets a policy variant retain the same classification rules without sharing event subscriptions.

qualifications: The predicates are reused by reference rather than duplicated; any behavior arising from mutable state captured by those functions is therefore still shared.

accounts.prose: The wrapper does not itself retry, delay, or turn a handled failure into the caller's final return value. RetryPolicy supplies that higher-level meaning: `{success}` ends its loop; `{error}` or `{value}` is passed to backoff as the last failure and may trigger another attempt. Once retries are unavailable, RetryPolicy rethrows the stored error for `{error}`, but returns the stored value for `{value}`. This explains why a result-filtered value is called a failure for policy decisions even though it can eventually be returned to the caller after give-up.

referent.description: How RetryPolicy consumes ExecuteWrapper's classified outcomes

qualifications: This consumer behavior is specific to the captured RetryPolicy implementation and is not intrinsic to ExecuteWrapper's union type.
RetryPolicy also stops retrying when its abort signal is set or its configured retry bound is reached.

accounts.prose: ExecuteWrapper owns fresh success/failure emitters and exposes their subscription functions. invoke awaits the callback. A value rejected by resultFilter becomes a handled failure `{value}`; any other value becomes `{success}`. A thrown error matching errorFilter becomes `{error}`; a nonmatching error is reported as unhandled and rethrown. clone preserves the two predicates but creates new emitters.

accounts.prose: ExecuteWrapper is a boundary around one attempted call: it normalizes outcomes that a policy is meant to handle into a discriminated object, while allowing an unhandled thrown error to remain an actual rejection. `invoke(fn, ...args)` awaits `fn(...args)`, so the same classification applies to direct return values and fulfilled promises. After fulfillment, `resultFilter(value) === false` produces `{ success: value }`; `true` treats the otherwise successful value as a handled failure and produces `{ value }`. If the attempted work throws or its promise rejects, `errorFilter(error) === true` converts that exception to `{ error }`; `false` emits an unhandled-failure notification when observed and then rethrows the original error. Thus “handled” means represented for policy-level processing, not necessarily that the overall operation ultimately succeeds. With the constructor defaults, no returned value is rejected by result filtering and no thrown error is handled.

accounts.prose: ExecuteWrapper is a boundary around one attempted call: it normalizes outcomes that a policy is meant to handle into a discriminated object, while allowing an unhandled thrown error to remain an actual rejection. `invoke(fn, ...args)` awaits `fn(...args)`, so the same classification applies to direct return values and fulfilled promises. After fulfillment, `resultFilter(value) === false` produces `{ success: value }`; `true` treats the otherwise successful value as a handled failure and produces `{ value }`. If the attempted work throws or its promise rejects, `errorFilter(error) === true` converts that exception to `{ error }`; `false` emits an unhandled-failure notification when observed and then rethrows the original error. Thus “handled” means represented for policy-level processing, not necessarily that the overall operation ultimately succeeds. With the constructor defaults, no returned value is rejected by result filtering and no thrown error is handled.

accounts.prose: The two public event properties are subscription functions, not the outcome itself. A success notification contains only elapsed `duration`. A failure notification contains `duration`, `handled`, and `reason`, where `reason` is `{ value }` for a filtered result or `{ error }` for an exception. For a filtered result, `handled` is always true. For an exception, it is the boolean returned by `errorFilter`, so an event can report `handled: false` immediately before `invoke` rethrows. Timing work is skipped entirely when both emitters have zero listeners at the start of the invocation; consequently, these events are observational and listener presence controls whether duration is measured. Subscriptions return disposables, and EventEmitter invokes current listeners synchronously.

referent.description: ExecuteWrapper success/failure event payloads and conditional duration measurement

qualifications: Listener count is sampled once, before the callback is invoked; adding a first listener during that callback does not retroactively enable timing for that invocation.

The duration covers the awaited callback plus subsequent result filtering up to the emission point, and is expressed in milliseconds by either `performance.now()` or a converted high-resolution process clock.

EventEmitter does not catch listener exceptions. In ExecuteWrapper, filtering and emission occur inside its `try`, so a throwing filter or listener can alter the apparent failure path; in particular, this code does not provide observer-exception isolation.

accounts.prose: The wrapper does not itself retry, delay, or turn a handled failure into the caller's final return value. RetryPolicy supplies that higher-level meaning: `{success}` ends its loop; `{error}` or `{value}` is passed to backoff as the last failure and may trigger another attempt. Once retries are unavailable, RetryPolicy rethrows the stored error for `{error}`, but returns the stored value for `{value}`. This explains why a result-filtered value is called a failure for policy decisions even though it can eventually be returned to the caller after give-up.

accounts.prose: ExecuteWrapper.invoke classifies the value caught by its single try/catch, not merely exceptions originating in the supplied callback. After awaiting the callback, failures from resultFilter, duration measurement on the success path, or synchronous success listeners enter the same catch and are passed to errorFilter. If that predicate returns true, invoke emits a handled failure event and resolves to an object containing the exact caught value as `error`; if it returns false, invoke emits an unhandled failure event and rethrows that same value. This sharpens, rather than overturns, the earlier account: classification has important boundaries and can itself be disrupted by predicates, timing, and listeners.

accounts.prose: Event notification is synchronous and has no listener-level exception isolation. A throwing success listener is caught by invoke and can cause a completed callback result to be discarded, passed to errorFilter as the listener's exception, and followed by a failure notification. By contrast, errorFilter and failure emission run inside the catch clause rather than inside another protective try: if errorFilter throws, its exception replaces the original caught value; if failure-duration evaluation or a failure listener throws, that later exception escapes and can prevent the selected `{ error }` result or original-value rethrow. With multiple listeners, EventEmitter stops iterating when one throws.

referent.description: Observer and classifier failures that alter ExecuteWrapper exception outcomes

qualifications: A failure event is attempted before either returning `{ error }` or rethrowing the unhandled value, provided timing evaluation and emission complete normally.
Listener registration changes during an awaited call can affect who receives an event, while the decision to collect timing and emit at all is fixed by listener counts at invocation start.
These edge cases follow control flow in the captured sources and are not covered by the supplied ExecuteWrapper test file.

accounts.prose: The catch domain starts at `await fn(...args)` and extends through result filtering, success-duration calculation, and success-event emission. It therefore handles both synchronous throws and awaited rejections from the callback, but it also reclassifies infrastructure failures from resultFilter or the success path as though they were operation errors. Stopwatch creation occurs before the try, so an exception while initially reading the clock bypasses errorFilter entirely.

accounts.prose: ExecuteWrapper owns fresh success/failure emitters and exposes their subscription functions. invoke awaits the callback. A value rejected by resultFilter becomes a handled failure `{value}`; any other value becomes `{success}`. A thrown error matching errorFilter becomes `{error}`; a nonmatching error is reported as unhandled and rethrown. clone preserves the two predicates but creates new emitters.

accounts.prose: ExecuteWrapper is a boundary around one attempted call: it normalizes outcomes that a policy is meant to handle into a discriminated object, while allowing an unhandled thrown error to remain an actual rejection. `invoke(fn, ...args)` awaits `fn(...args)`, so the same classification applies to direct return values and fulfilled promises. After fulfillment, `resultFilter(value) === false` produces `{ success: value }`; `true` treats the otherwise successful value as a handled failure and produces `{ value }`. If the attempted work throws or its promise rejects, `errorFilter(error) === true` converts that exception to `{ error }`; `false` emits an unhandled-failure notification when observed and then rethrows the original error. Thus “handled” means represented for policy-level processing, not necessarily that the overall operation ultimately succeeds. With the constructor defaults, no returned value is rejected by result filtering and no thrown error is handled.

accounts.prose: ExecuteWrapper is a boundary around one attempted call: it normalizes outcomes that a policy is meant to handle into a discriminated object, while allowing an unhandled thrown error to remain an actual rejection. `invoke(fn, ...args)` awaits `fn(...args)`, so the same classification applies to direct return values and fulfilled promises. After fulfillment, `resultFilter(value) === false` produces `{ success: value }`; `true` treats the otherwise successful value as a handled failure and produces `{ value }`. If the attempted work throws or its promise rejects, `errorFilter(error) === true` converts that exception to `{ error }`; `false` emits an unhandled-failure notification when observed and then rethrows the original error. Thus “handled” means represented for policy-level processing, not necessarily that the overall operation ultimately succeeds. With the constructor defaults, no returned value is rejected by result filtering and no thrown error is handled.

qualifications: This describes the captured TypeScript implementation; source text alone does not establish behavior in every built or deployed version.
The ordinary outcome flow assumes the supplied filters and event listeners do not themselves throw; those callbacks are not isolated from `invoke`'s control flow.
`await` assimilates native promises and other PromiseLike results before result filtering.

accounts.prose: The two public event properties are subscription functions, not the outcome itself. A success notification contains only elapsed `duration`. A failure notification contains `duration`, `handled`, and `reason`, where `reason` is `{ value }` for a filtered result or `{ error }` for an exception. For a filtered result, `handled` is always true. For an exception, it is the boolean returned by `errorFilter`, so an event can report `handled: false` immediately before `invoke` rethrows. Timing work is skipped entirely when both emitters have zero listeners at the start of the invocation; consequently, these events are observational and listener presence controls whether duration is measured. Subscriptions return disposables, and EventEmitter invokes current listeners synchronously.

referent.description: ExecuteWrapper success/failure event payloads and conditional duration measurement

qualifications: Listener count is sampled once, before the callback is invoked; adding a first listener during that callback does not retroactively enable timing for that invocation.

The duration covers the awaited callback plus subsequent result filtering up to the emission point, and is expressed in milliseconds by either `performance.now()` or a converted high-resolution process clock.

EventEmitter does not catch listener exceptions. In ExecuteWrapper, filtering and emission occur inside its `try`, so a throwing filter or listener can alter the apparent failure path; in particular, this code does not provide observer-exception isolation.

accounts.prose: The wrapper does not itself retry, delay, or turn a handled failure into the caller's final return value. RetryPolicy supplies that higher-level meaning: `{success}` ends its loop; `{error}` or `{value}` is passed to backoff as the last failure and may trigger another attempt. Once retries are unavailable, RetryPolicy rethrows the stored error for `{error}`, but returns the stored value for `{value}`. This explains why a result-filtered value is called a failure for policy decisions even though it can eventually be returned to the caller after give-up.

qualifications: This consumer behavior is specific to the captured RetryPolicy implementation and is not intrinsic to ExecuteWrapper's union type.
RetryPolicy also stops retrying when its abort signal is set or its configured retry bound is reached.

@investigram-da67d827 · interpretation
ExecuteWrapper.invoke classifies the value caught by its single try/catch, not merely exceptions originating in the supplied callback. After awaiting the callback, failures from resultFilter, duration measurement on the success path, or synchronous success listeners enter the same catch and are passed to errorFilter. If that predicate returns true, invoke emits a handled failure event and resolves to an object containing the exact caught value as `error`; if it returns false, invoke emits an unhandled failure event and rethrows that same value. This sharpens, rather than overturns, the earlier account: classification has important boundaries and can itself be disrupted by predicates, timing, and listeners.
Referent: Deep examination of ExecuteWrapper exception classification and its boundaries

  Qualification: The true/false wording follows the declared boolean predicate contract; ordinary JavaScript branching would in practice use the returned value's truthiness if the contract were violated.
  Qualification: The exact caught value is preserved only while errorFilter, failure-duration evaluation, and failure emission complete normally.

@investigram-92cfd159 · interpretation
Event notification is synchronous and has no listener-level exception isolation. A throwing success listener is caught by invoke and can cause a completed callback result to be discarded, passed to errorFilter as the listener's exception, and followed by a failure notification. By contrast, errorFilter and failure emission run inside the catch clause rather than inside another protective try: if errorFilter throws, its exception replaces the original caught value; if failure-duration evaluation or a failure listener throws, that later exception escapes and can prevent the selected `{ error }` result or original-value rethrow. With multiple listeners, EventEmitter stops iterating when one throws.

accounts.prose: ExecuteWrapper owns fresh success/failure emitters and exposes their subscription functions. invoke awaits the callback. A value rejected by resultFilter becomes a handled failure `{value}`; any other value becomes `{success}`. A thrown error matching errorFilter becomes `{error}`; a nonmatching error is reported as unhandled and rethrown. clone preserves the two predicates but creates new emitters.

accounts.prose: ExecuteWrapper is a boundary around one attempted call: it normalizes outcomes that a policy is meant to handle into a discriminated object, while allowing an unhandled thrown error to remain an actual rejection. `invoke(fn, ...args)` awaits `fn(...args)`, so the same classification applies to direct return values and fulfilled promises. After fulfillment, `resultFilter(value) === false` produces `{ success: value }`; `true` treats the otherwise successful value as a handled failure and produces `{ value }`. If the attempted work throws or its promise rejects, `errorFilter(error) === true` converts that exception to `{ error }`; `false` emits an unhandled-failure notification when observed and then rethrows the original error. Thus “handled” means represented for policy-level processing, not necessarily that the overall operation ultimately succeeds. With the constructor defaults, no returned value is rejected by result filtering and no thrown error is handled.

accounts.prose: ExecuteWrapper is a boundary around one attempted call: it normalizes outcomes that a policy is meant to handle into a discriminated object, while allowing an unhandled thrown error to remain an actual rejection. `invoke(fn, ...args)` awaits `fn(...args)`, so the same classification applies to direct return values and fulfilled promises. After fulfillment, `resultFilter(value) === false` produces `{ success: value }`; `true` treats the otherwise successful value as a handled failure and produces `{ value }`. If the attempted work throws or its promise rejects, `errorFilter(error) === true` converts that exception to `{ error }`; `false` emits an unhandled-failure notification when observed and then rethrows the original error. Thus “handled” means represented for policy-level processing, not necessarily that the overall operation ultimately succeeds. With the constructor defaults, no returned value is rejected by result filtering and no thrown error is handled.

referent.description: Clarified ExecuteWrapper invocation, outcome classification, observability, and cloning behavior

qualifications: This describes the captured TypeScript implementation; source text alone does not establish behavior in every built or deployed version.
The ordinary outcome flow assumes the supplied filters and event listeners do not themselves throw; those callbacks are not isolated from `invoke`'s control flow.
`await` assimilates native promises and other PromiseLike results before result filtering.

accounts.prose: The two public event properties are subscription functions, not the outcome itself. A success notification contains only elapsed `duration`. A failure notification contains `duration`, `handled`, and `reason`, where `reason` is `{ value }` for a filtered result or `{ error }` for an exception. For a filtered result, `handled` is always true. For an exception, it is the boolean returned by `errorFilter`, so an event can report `handled: false` immediately before `invoke` rethrows. Timing work is skipped entirely when both emitters have zero listeners at the start of the invocation; consequently, these events are observational and listener presence controls whether duration is measured. Subscriptions return disposables, and EventEmitter invokes current listeners synchronously.

referent.description: ExecuteWrapper success/failure event payloads and conditional duration measurement

qualifications: Listener count is sampled once, before the callback is invoked; adding a first listener during that callback does not retroactively enable timing for that invocation.

The duration covers the awaited callback plus subsequent result filtering up to the emission point, and is expressed in milliseconds by either `performance.now()` or a converted high-resolution process clock.

EventEmitter does not catch listener exceptions. In ExecuteWrapper, filtering and emission occur inside its `try`, so a throwing filter or listener can alter the apparent failure path; in particular, this code does not provide observer-exception isolation.

accounts.prose: `clone()` copies configuration but not observation state. It constructs a new ExecuteWrapper with the same `errorFilter` and `resultFilter` function objects. Because each instance initializes its own success and failure emitters, listeners attached to the original are not attached to the clone. This lets a policy variant retain the same classification rules without sharing event subscriptions.

referent.description: ExecuteWrapper clone configuration and listener isolation

qualifications: The predicates are reused by reference rather than duplicated; any behavior arising from mutable state captured by those functions is therefore still shared.
Fresh emitter state follows from constructing a new instance whose emitter fields are initialized per instance.

accounts.prose: The wrapper does not itself retry, delay, or turn a handled failure into the caller's final return value. RetryPolicy supplies that higher-level meaning: `{success}` ends its loop; `{error}` or `{value}` is passed to backoff as the last failure and may trigger another attempt. Once retries are unavailable, RetryPolicy rethrows the stored error for `{error}`, but returns the stored value for `{value}`. This explains why a result-filtered value is called a failure for policy decisions even though it can eventually be returned to the caller after give-up.

referent.description: How RetryPolicy consumes ExecuteWrapper's classified outcomes

qualifications: This consumer behavior is specific to the captured RetryPolicy implementation and is not intrinsic to ExecuteWrapper's union type.
RetryPolicy also stops retrying when its abort signal is set or its configured retry bound is reached.

accounts.prose: ExecuteWrapper is a boundary around one attempted call: it normalizes outcomes that a policy is meant to handle into a discriminated object, while allowing an unhandled thrown error to remain an actual rejection. `invoke(fn, ...args)` awaits `fn(...args)`, so the same classification applies to direct return values and fulfilled promises. After fulfillment, `resultFilter(value) === false` produces `{ success: value }`; `true` treats the otherwise successful value as a handled failure and produces `{ value }`. If the attempted work throws or its promise rejects, `errorFilter(error) === true` converts that exception to `{ error }`; `false` emits an unhandled-failure notification when observed and then rethrows the original error. Thus “handled” means represented for policy-level processing, not necessarily that the overall operation ultimately succeeds. With the constructor defaults, no returned value is rejected by result filtering and no thrown error is handled.

accounts.prose: ExecuteWrapper is a boundary around one attempted call: it normalizes outcomes that a policy is meant to handle into a discriminated object, while allowing an unhandled thrown error to remain an actual rejection. `invoke(fn, ...args)` awaits `fn(...args)`, so the same classification applies to direct return values and fulfilled promises. After fulfillment, `resultFilter(value) === false` produces `{ success: value }`; `true` treats the otherwise successful value as a handled failure and produces `{ value }`. If the attempted work throws or its promise rejects, `errorFilter(error) === true` converts that exception to `{ error }`; `false` emits an unhandled-failure notification when observed and then rethrows the original error. Thus “handled” means represented for policy-level processing, not necessarily that the overall operation ultimately succeeds. With the constructor defaults, no returned value is rejected by result filtering and no thrown error is handled.

`await` assimilates native promises and other PromiseLike results before result filtering.

accounts.prose: The two public event properties are subscription functions, not the outcome itself. A success notification contains only elapsed `duration`. A failure notification contains `duration`, `handled`, and `reason`, where `reason` is `{ value }` for a filtered result or `{ error }` for an exception. For a filtered result, `handled` is always true. For an exception, it is the boolean returned by `errorFilter`, so an event can report `handled: false` immediately before `invoke` rethrows. Timing work is skipped entirely when both emitters have zero listeners at the start of the invocation; consequently, these events are observational and listener presence controls whether duration is measured. Subscriptions return disposables, and EventEmitter invokes current listeners synchronously.

referent.description: ExecuteWrapper success/failure event payloads and conditional duration measurement

qualifications: Listener count is sampled once, before the callback is invoked; adding a first listener during that callback does not retroactively enable timing for that invocation.

The duration covers the awaited callback plus subsequent result filtering up to the emission point, and is expressed in milliseconds by either `performance.now()` or a converted high-resolution process clock.

EventEmitter does not catch listener exceptions. In ExecuteWrapper, filtering and emission occur inside its `try`, so a throwing filter or listener can alter the apparent failure path; in particular, this code does not provide observer-exception isolation.

accounts.prose: `clone()` copies configuration but not observation state. It constructs a new ExecuteWrapper with the same `errorFilter` and `resultFilter` function objects. Because each instance initializes its own success and failure emitters, listeners attached to the original are not attached to the clone. This lets a policy variant retain the same classification rules without sharing event subscriptions.

accounts.prose: The wrapper does not itself retry, delay, or turn a handled failure into the caller's final return value. RetryPolicy supplies that higher-level meaning: `{success}` ends its loop; `{error}` or `{value}` is passed to backoff as the last failure and may trigger another attempt. Once retries are unavailable, RetryPolicy rethrows the stored error for `{error}`, but returns the stored value for `{value}`. This explains why a result-filtered value is called a failure for policy decisions even though it can eventually be returned to the caller after give-up.

qualifications: This consumer behavior is specific to the captured RetryPolicy implementation and is not intrinsic to ExecuteWrapper's union type.
RetryPolicy also stops retrying when its abort signal is set or its configured retry bound is reached.

accounts.prose: ExecuteWrapper is a boundary around one attempted call: it normalizes outcomes that a policy is meant to handle into a discriminated object, while allowing an unhandled thrown error to remain an actual rejection. `invoke(fn, ...args)` awaits `fn(...args)`, so the same classification applies to direct return values and fulfilled promises. After fulfillment, `resultFilter(value) === false` produces `{ success: value }`; `true` treats the otherwise successful value as a handled failure and produces `{ value }`. If the attempted work throws or its promise rejects, `errorFilter(error) === true` converts that exception to `{ error }`; `false` emits an unhandled-failure notification when observed and then rethrows the original error. Thus “handled” means represented for policy-level processing, not necessarily that the overall operation ultimately succeeds. With the constructor defaults, no returned value is rejected by result filtering and no thrown error is handled.

referent.description: Clarified ExecuteWrapper invocation, outcome classification, observability, and cloning behavior

qualifications: This describes the captured TypeScript implementation; source text alone does not establish behavior in every built or deployed version.
The ordinary outcome flow assumes the supplied filters and event listeners do not themselves throw; those callbacks are not isolated from `invoke`'s control flow.
`await` assimilates native promises and other PromiseLike results before result filtering.

accounts.prose: The two public event properties are subscription functions, not the outcome itself. A success notification contains only elapsed `duration`. A failure notification contains `duration`, `handled`, and `reason`, where `reason` is `{ value }` for a filtered result or `{ error }` for an exception. For a filtered result, `handled` is always true. For an exception, it is the boolean returned by `errorFilter`, so an event can report `handled: false` immediately before `invoke` rethrows. Timing work is skipped entirely when both emitters have zero listeners at the start of the invocation; consequently, these events are observational and listener presence controls whether duration is measured. Subscriptions return disposables, and EventEmitter invokes current listeners synchronously.

referent.description: ExecuteWrapper success/failure event payloads and conditional duration measurement

qualifications: Listener count is sampled once, before the callback is invoked; adding a first listener during that callback does not retroactively enable timing for that invocation.

The duration covers the awaited callback plus subsequent result filtering up to the emission point, and is expressed in milliseconds by either `performance.now()` or a converted high-resolution process clock.

EventEmitter does not catch listener exceptions. In ExecuteWrapper, filtering and emission occur inside its `try`, so a throwing filter or listener can alter the apparent failure path; in particular, this code does not provide observer-exception isolation.

accounts.prose: The wrapper does not itself retry, delay, or turn a handled failure into the caller's final return value. RetryPolicy supplies that higher-level meaning: `{success}` ends its loop; `{error}` or `{value}` is passed to backoff as the last failure and may trigger another attempt. Once retries are unavailable, RetryPolicy rethrows the stored error for `{error}`, but returns the stored value for `{value}`. This explains why a result-filtered value is called a failure for policy decisions even though it can eventually be returned to the caller after give-up.

qualifications: This consumer behavior is specific to the captured RetryPolicy implementation and is not intrinsic to ExecuteWrapper's union type.

accounts.prose: ExecuteWrapper owns fresh success/failure emitters and exposes their subscription functions. invoke awaits the callback. A value rejected by resultFilter becomes a handled failure `{value}`; any other value becomes `{success}`. A thrown error matching errorFilter becomes `{error}`; a nonmatching error is reported as unhandled and rethrown. clone preserves the two predicates but creates new emitters.

qualifications: “Fresh emitters” follows construction of a new ExecuteWrapper in clone; filter functions themselves are reused.
The callback may be synchronous or promise-like because its result is awaited.
